newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel cabinet in crisis; poll backs change.
newsitem.headline: Israel cabinet in crisis; poll backs change.

text.p: Israel's most enduring agitator, Foreign Minister David Levy, has again turned a quarrel into a national political crisis.
On Monday Levy brought Benjamin Netanyahu's government to its knees, threatening to quit over the prime minister's leadership and push the coalition to the edge of collapse.
If a new opinion poll was any indication, Levy this time touched a resonant chord with his countrymen. The poll showed three-quarters of Israelis want a change in government.
"In the coming days I will decide on my next moves, on my continuing membership in the government," Levy, 59, told a hastily called news conference after days of silence.
A veteran of brinkmanship who has more than 28 years in Israel's parliament, 17 in government, Levy accused Netanyahu of keeping him in the dark on important issues.
Netanyahu, a 47-year-old right-winger who came to power a year ago, reiterated his faith in Levy and promised to work to resolve their dispute.
But Levy's threat underscored growing disenchantment with Netanyahu's way of running his government along with a more than three-month-old crisis in peace talks with Palestinians.
"It's just like a kindergarten with the prime minister on the level of a kindergarten teacher," said Deputy Minister Shlomo Benizri.
A media disclosure on Friday that National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon had secretly met top PLO official Mahmoud Abbas triggered Levy's threat to resign.
"The question is, whether as foreign minister I should know things after the fact," said Levy, a white-haired father of 12 and construction worker by trade.
Levy said his Gesher faction, with five of the 66 coalition seats in the 120-member parliament, had joined Netanyahu to advance peace and improve life for low-income Israelis.
"I am sorry to say that a year after the government was established, the peace process is stuck and the social situation has deteriorated," Levy said.
Two ministers have already quit the cabinet. Netanyahu had hoped to get parliamentary approval on Monday for Sharon to replace one of them, Dan Meridor, as finance minister.
But Levy balked at Sharon's demand to join Levy, the prime minister and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai in an inner cabinet team that shapes peace policy.
The Teleseker poll for Israel's Channel One television showed that nearly 75 percent of Israelis would like to see a change in the makeup of the government.
"This is certainly a red light for the government," said Dori Shadmon, who organised the poll for Israel's Channel One TV.
The survey of 500 Israelis showed 22.3 percent favoured the government's continued existence while 43.9 percent wanted early elections and 31.0 percent a national unity government.
If Levy was to take Gesher out of the government, Netanyahu's fate would depend on an unstable parliamentary majority of one built on rebellious Likud members threatening to bolt.
The Labour party's Shimon Peres, ousted by Netanyahu, doubted the coalition would vote itself out of power. "I don't see all of these guys running to elections," he said.

But Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani, leader of the right-centre Third Way party in the coalition, wasn't taking any chances. He said his four-member faction was preparing for the possibility of elections.
